paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Brownian motion is the random movement of particles suspended in a liquid or a gas. It is named after the Scottish botanist Robert Brown, who described it in 1827. In mathematics, the usual way to describe it is the Wiener process, which is itself often just called Brownian motion.

paragraphs.heading: What Brown saw
paragraphs.text: Brown was studying how plants reproduce when he looked at pollen grains of Clarkia pulchella in water under a simple microscope. The grains hold particles about 6.4 microns (1/4,000th of an inch) across, and he watched them jiggle without stopping. He repeated the test with lifeless matter such as glass and rock dust. That ruled out life as the cause, though the physical reason was still unexplained.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein's explanation
paragraphs.text: In 1905 Albert Einstein modelled the pollen particles as being pushed by individual water molecules. The direction of these hits keeps changing, and at any moment one side may be struck more than the other, so the particle seems to move at random. At the time, whether atoms and molecules truly existed was still fiercely argued. His account became convincing evidence that they do.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring atoms
paragraphs.text: The first step in Einstein's argument was to work out the distance a Brownian particle covers over a set time. Classical mechanics cannot answer that, because the particle suffers roughly 10¹⁴ collisions every second. Einstein instead built a diffusion equation for the particles, and through it he could find the size of atoms and how many atoms are in a mole of gas. Jean Perrin's careful experiments in 1908 confirmed these predictions, settled the debate over atoms, and led to his Nobel Prize in Physics in 1926.

paragraphs.heading: The mathematics
paragraphs.text: In his 1900 doctoral thesis, The Theory of Speculation, Louis Bachelier modelled this random process while analysing the stock and option markets. His work tying random walks to continuous time stayed largely unknown until the 1950s. In 1923 Norbert Wiener gave the first complete and rigorous mathematical treatment, which is why the idea is now called the Wiener process.

paragraphs.heading: Why chance is the only tool
paragraphs.text: The motion comes from many molecules interacting at once, and no model can follow every one of them. So only probability models applied to whole populations of molecules can describe it. Both simpler and more complex random processes, such as random walks, approach Brownian motion in the limit. In 2010 researchers managed for the first time to measure, for one Brownian particle, its velocity at a single instant: the particle was a glass bead held in air by optical tweezers, and the data matched the Maxwell–Boltzmann velocity distribution.
